sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 77 in full with each verse's related passages before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Scripture is never stored in the notes; it loads from the bundled BSB.

study.title: I will remember Your wonders
study.intro: Asaph cries through a sleepless night, asking if God has forgotten to be gracious, then turns his mind to God's mighty deeds of old, above all the Exodus through the sea.
study.context: Psalm 77 is headed 'For the choirmaster. According to Jeduthun. A Psalm of Asaph.' Jeduthun was one of David's chief musicians (1 Chronicles 16:41). The psalm has two halves. Verses 1–9 are a lament full of sleepless questions; verse 10 is the turning point; verses 11–20 recall God's works, ending with the Red Sea crossing told as a thunderstorm. It shows a pattern for faith in dark seasons: honest complaint, then deliberate remembering.
study.peopleNote: The heading names Asaph and Jeduthun, Levite musicians appointed by David; the app has no profiles for them, so no person card is linked for them. Verse 15 names the sons of Jacob and Joseph, and verse 20 names Moses and Aaron, who have profiles in the app. Planned paintings would show night scenes, storms and the sea path; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: I cried aloud
verses.heading: A voice raised to God
verses.meaning: The heading names the choirmaster, Jeduthun and Asaph. Then the psalmist begins: 'I cried out to God; I cried aloud to God to hear me.' He does not pray politely or quietly. He uses his voice and calls out, repeating himself because the need is so great. The psalms give us permission to bring our raw distress to God. Faith is not pretending things are fine; it is directing our cry toward the One who can hear.
verses.context: Jeduthun led music with Heman and Asaph (1 Chronicles 16:41-42) and also appears in the headings of Psalms 39 and 62. Hebrews 5:7 says Jesus offered prayers with loud cries and tears.
explore: Jeduthun
A Levite musician under David whose name may mark a choir or a musical style used for this psalm.
Cried aloud
Literally 'my voice to God,' an urgent spoken prayer rather than a silent thought.
verses.reflect: What would it look like for you to bring your honest cry to God today?
verses.alt: A villager in a head cloth standing on a dark rooftop with face lifted to the night sky.

verses.title: Hands outstretched all night
verses.heading: A soul that would not be comforted
verses.meaning: Verse 2 says: 'In the day of trouble I sought the Lord; through the night my outstretched hands did not grow weary; my soul refused to be comforted.' The trouble is long, stretching from day into night. He keeps praying with lifted hands. Yet comfort does not come; his soul will not accept easy answers. This is the honesty of grief. Sometimes we seek God and still hurt, and the psalm tells us that is not a failure of faith.
verses.context: Genesis 37:35 says Jacob refused to be comforted over Joseph. Jeremiah 31:15 describes Rachel refusing comfort for her children. Matthew 5:4 says those who mourn will be comforted.
explore: Day of trouble
A time of distress or crisis, a phrase often used in the psalms for seasons of pain.
Outstretched hands
Hands spread out or lifted in prayer, a common posture of pleading in Israel.
verses.reflect: Is there a grief you have kept praying about that still feels unanswered?
verses.alt: An oil lamp burning low beside a mat where a person kneels with hands raised.

verses.title: I groaned
verses.heading: Remembering God hurts
verses.meaning: Verse 3 says: 'I remembered You, O God, and I groaned; I mused and my spirit grew faint. Selah.' Surprisingly, thinking about God first makes things worse. Remembering who God is, and comparing it to his present pain, makes him groan. The more he thinks, the weaker he feels. This is the honest middle of lament, before the turn. The Selah marks a pause in that heavy place, letting us sit with it rather than rush past it.
verses.context: Psalm 42:4 recalls past worship with a heavy heart. Romans 8:26 says the Spirit intercedes with groans too deep for words. Psalm 143:4 says 'my spirit faints within me.'
explore: Mused
To meditate or think over something repeatedly; here the reflection leads to complaint.
Grew faint
To be weak, overwhelmed or wrapped in weariness, like someone fainting from exhaustion.
verses.reflect: Have you ever found that thinking about God made your questions sharper? How did you handle it?
verses.alt: A person sitting on a stone bench in moonlight with head bowed into folded arms.

verses.title: Too troubled to speak
verses.heading: A sleepless night
verses.meaning: Verse 4 says: 'You have kept my eyes from closing; I am too troubled to speak.' The psalmist even sees his sleeplessness as coming from God's hand. He cannot rest, and his distress is so great that words fail. Many who suffer know nights like this, when the mind races and prayers dry up. The psalm does not shame such nights. It names them before God, and in naming them begins to find the way through.
verses.context: Psalm 6:6 speaks of flooding the bed with tears. Esther 6:1 tells of a king who could not sleep. Psalm 4:8 later says, 'I will lie down and sleep in peace.'
explore: Kept my eyes from closing
Literally 'You held the lids of my eyes,' as if God kept them open.
Too troubled
Deeply agitated or disturbed, unable to put feelings into speech.
verses.reflect: When you can't sleep for worry, what helps you turn toward God?
verses.alt: A dark room with a small window showing stars and a sleeper lying awake.

verses.title: Days of old
verses.heading: Looking back in time
verses.meaning: Verse 5 says: 'I considered the days of old, the years long in the past.' In his distress, he starts to think about history. At first this may be painful nostalgia, comparing better days with present darkness. But this backward look will become the key to his recovery. The past holds the record of what God has done. When the present is confusing, memory of God's earlier faithfulness gives us somewhere to stand.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 32:7 says, 'Remember the days of old; consider the years long past.' Psalm 143:5 says, 'I remember the days of old; I meditate on all Your works.'
explore: Considered
Thought carefully about, weighed and reflected on, as one turns a matter over in the mind.
Days of old
The earlier history of God's people, especially the time of the Exodus and wilderness.
verses.reflect: What past moment of God's faithfulness could you recall when today feels dark?
verses.alt: An old man in a head cloth unrolling a scroll by lamplight.

verses.title: My song in the night
verses.heading: A heart searching
verses.meaning: Verse 6 says: 'At night I remembered my song; in my heart I mused, and my spirit pondered:' He recalls songs he once sang to God, perhaps in happier times. The memory leads to deep searching. His spirit digs for answers, and the colon at the end introduces the hard questions he is about to ask. Remembering past joy can raise painful questions, but it also keeps a thread connecting us to the God we once praised.
verses.context: Job 35:10 speaks of God who gives songs in the night. Psalm 42:8 says His song is with me at night. Acts 16:25 tells of Paul and Silas singing hymns at midnight in prison.
explore: My song
A song of praise the psalmist once sang, perhaps with music on the stringed instrument.
Pondered
Searched diligently, like someone digging or seeking for something hidden.
verses.reflect: What song of faith from an earlier season of life still speaks to you?
verses.alt: A small harp leaning against a wall beside a sleeping mat in moonlight.

verses.title: Spurned forever?
verses.heading: The first hard question
verses.meaning: Verse 7 begins the questions: '“Will the Lord spurn us forever and never show His favor again?”' He fears that God's rejection might be permanent. Will the good days never return? This is not unbelief; he is asking God, not walking away. Bringing our worst fears into words before God is itself an act of faith. The question also contains its own hint of hope: it contrasts God's present silence with His known character of favor.
verses.context: Lamentations 3:31-32 answers that the Lord will not cast off forever; though He brings grief, He will show compassion. Psalm 74:1 asks why God has rejected His people forever.
explore: Spurn
To reject or cast off, as one might push away something unwanted.
Favor
God's goodwill and kindness, shown in blessing and acceptance of His people.
verses.reflect: What fear about God's attitude toward you do you need to bring into words before Him?
verses.alt: A closed wooden door in a stone wall at dusk with no light within.

verses.title: Loving devotion gone?
verses.heading: Has the promise failed?
verses.meaning: Verse 8 continues: 'Is His loving devotion gone forever? Has His promise failed for all time?' He touches the deepest foundations: God's steadfast covenant love and His spoken promise. If those could fail, there would be no hope at all. The questions are almost unthinkable, which is why they hurt so much. Yet by naming God's loving devotion and His promise, the psalmist is reminding himself of exactly what God has said He would be.
verses.context: Lamentations 3:22 says the LORD's loving devotion never ceases. Joshua 21:45 says not one of God's good promises failed. Numbers 23:19 says God is not a man that He should lie.
explore: Loving devotion
The Hebrew hesed, God's faithful covenant love that keeps commitment even when undeserved.
Promise
God's spoken word, His pledged commitment to His people.
verses.reflect: Which promise of God do you most need reassurance about right now?
verses.alt: A worn scroll lying open on a table with a lamp guttering beside it.

verses.title: Forgotten to be gracious?
verses.heading: Anger and compassion
verses.meaning: Verse 9 finishes the questions: '“Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has His anger shut off His compassion?” Selah.' He wonders whether God's anger has closed the door on mercy. The picture is of compassion locked away. These are the questions of a heart in darkness. The Selah marks the bottom of the lament. From here the psalm will begin to climb, but only after letting these questions be fully spoken before God.
verses.context: Exodus 34:6 describes the LORD as compassionate and gracious, slow to anger. Isaiah 49:15 says a mother may forget her child, but God will not forget. Psalm 103:8-9 says He will not always accuse.
explore: Gracious
Showing undeserved favor and kindness, a core part of God's revealed character.
Shut off
Closed up or shut in, as if compassion were locked away behind anger.
verses.reflect: What does Exodus 34:6 tell you about God when you feel He has forgotten you?
verses.alt: A shuttered window in a dark house with the faint first light of dawn on the horizon.

verses.title: The right hand changed
verses.heading: The turning point
verses.meaning: Verse 10 says: 'So I said, “I am grieved that the right hand of the Most High has changed.”' Here the psalmist names the heart of his pain: it seems God's powerful hand no longer acts for His people as before. This honest statement is the hinge of the psalm. Having said it, he will choose a different path. Naming exactly what hurts often clears the way to turn our minds toward truth, rather than staying stuck in the question.
verses.context: This verse can be read differently, as 'I will appeal to the years of the right hand of the Most High.' Either way it leads into remembering. Exodus 15:6 praises the LORD's right hand, majestic in power.
explore: Right hand
A symbol of strength and action; God's right hand is His power at work.
Most High
A title for God emphasizing that He is supreme over all powers and nations.
verses.reflect: What exactly is your grief or question, if you put it into one honest sentence?
verses.alt: A narrow mountain path at a fork with first light falling on one way.

verses.title: I will remember
verses.heading: Choosing to recall God's works
verses.meaning: Verse 11 marks the turn: 'I will remember the works of the LORD; yes, I will remember Your wonders of old.' Notice the repeated 'I will.' Remembering becomes a decision, not just a feeling. Earlier, memory made him groan; now he deliberately remembers God's acts. And he switches from speaking about God to speaking to Him: 'Your wonders.' This is a key to surviving dark seasons. We choose to rehearse what God has truly done.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 8:2 tells Israel to remember how the LORD led them. Psalm 103:2 says, 'Forget not all His kind deeds.' 1 Corinthians 11:24 records Jesus saying, 'Do this in remembrance of Me.'
explore: Works
God's actions in history, especially His acts of rescue and judgment.
Wonders
Extraordinary deeds that cause amazement, such as the plagues and the parting of the sea.
verses.reflect: What three works of God could you deliberately remember today?
verses.alt: Morning light spilling across hills as a person sits up and looks out at the view.

verses.title: Ponder Your mighty deeds
verses.heading: Meditation that heals
verses.meaning: Verse 12 says: 'I will reflect on all You have done and ponder Your mighty deeds.' He goes beyond a quick memory to slow, careful meditation. The same word for musing that earlier led him to complain now leads him to praise, because the subject has changed. Instead of turning over his own pain, he turns over God's deeds. What we dwell on shapes our hearts, and meditating on God's acts steadies a troubled soul.
verses.context: Philippians 4:8 urges us to think on whatever is true and praiseworthy. Psalm 145:5 says, 'I will meditate on Your wondrous works.' Psalm 1:2 speaks of meditating on God's law day and night.
explore: Reflect
To meditate, murmur or speak quietly to oneself about something.
Mighty deeds
Great and powerful acts that only God could do, such as the plagues and the Exodus.
verses.reflect: What would change if you spent ten minutes thinking about God's deeds rather than your worries?
verses.alt: A person sitting under an olive tree reading a scroll in calm afternoon light.

verses.title: Your way is holy
verses.heading: No god so great
verses.meaning: Verse 13 says: 'Your way, O God, is holy. What god is so great as our God?' Meditation leads to praise. God's way, His manner of acting, is holy, set apart and perfect, even when we do not understand it. The question 'What god is so great?' expects the answer: none. Compared to every other power or idol, the God of Israel stands alone. Seeing God's greatness puts our questions in a larger frame.
verses.context: Exodus 15:11 asks, 'Who among the gods is like You, O LORD? Who is like You, majestic in holiness?' Isaiah 55:9 says God's ways are higher than our ways.
explore: Holy
Set apart, pure and wholly other; God's holiness marks everything He does.
Way
God's path or manner of acting in the world and with His people.
verses.reflect: Where do you need to trust that God's way is holy even when you can't see the reason?
verses.alt: A straight road running through golden fields toward distant hills under a clear sky.

verses.title: God who works wonders
verses.heading: Strength shown to the nations
verses.meaning: Verse 14 says: 'You are the God who works wonders; You display Your strength among the peoples.' God is not only great in theory; He acts. His wonders are public, seen by the nations around Israel. Egypt and Canaan heard what He did. The God who seemed silent in verses 7–9 is the same God who has shown His strength openly before. That track record is the ground for trusting Him in the present silence.
verses.context: Exodus 9:16 says God raised up Pharaoh to show His power. Joshua 2:10 has Rahab say the Canaanites heard how the LORD dried up the Red Sea. Psalm 98:2 says He revealed His righteousness to the nations.
explore: Display
To make known or cause to be seen openly, so that others recognize who has acted.
Peoples
The nations and peoples of the world beyond Israel.
verses.reflect: How has God's strength been visible in your life to people around you?
verses.alt: Distant tents of many nations on a plain watching a great light over the hills.

verses.title: Redeemed with power
verses.heading: Sons of Jacob and Joseph
verses.meaning: Verse 15 says: 'With power You redeemed Your people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph. Selah.' The psalmist recalls the Exodus, when God rescued Israel from slavery in Egypt. 'Redeemed' means bought back or set free, often at a cost. Jacob and Joseph are named because the whole family, including the northern tribes descended from Joseph, came out together. The Selah invites us to pause on this great rescue, the foundation of Israel's faith.
verses.context: Exodus 6:6 says, 'I will redeem you with an outstretched arm.' Genesis 46:27 tells how Jacob's family went down to Egypt. 1 Peter 1:18-19 says we were redeemed with the precious blood of Christ.
explore: Redeemed
Set free or bought back, like a relative paying to free a family member from slavery.
Jacob and Joseph
Jacob was Israel's father; Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh became major tribes.
verses.reflect: What has God redeemed you from, and how do you remember it?
verses.alt: A long line of families with donkeys and bundles leaving a land of brick buildings at dawn.

verses.title: The waters saw You
verses.heading: The sea trembles
verses.meaning: Verse 16 says: 'The waters saw You, O God; the waters saw You and swirled; even the depths were shaken.' The psalmist pictures the Red Sea as if it had eyes. When it saw its Maker approach, it writhed and trembled. The deep waters, often a symbol of chaos in the ancient world, could not stand before God. What terrified Israel trembled before their God. No chaos in our lives is beyond His command.
verses.context: Exodus 14:21 says the LORD drove the sea back with a strong east wind. Psalm 114:3 says the sea looked and fled. Mark 4:39 shows Jesus rebuking the wind and waves.
explore: Swirled
Writhed or trembled, a word used for the pangs of labor or shaking in fear.
Depths
The deep waters of the sea, often a picture of chaos and danger.
verses.reflect: What 'deep waters' in your life need to see and tremble before God?
verses.alt: Churning dark sea waves pulling back from a rocky shore under heavy clouds.

verses.title: Arrows flashed
verses.heading: Storm over the sea
verses.meaning: Verse 17 says: 'The clouds poured down water; the skies resounded with thunder; Your arrows flashed back and forth.' The crossing is described as a mighty thunderstorm. Rain pours, thunder roars, and lightning bolts like arrows streak across the sky. Exodus does not describe this storm in detail, but the psalm draws on the language of God's power over creation. The God who shatters enemies' arrows in Psalm 76 fires His own in this storm.
verses.context: Exodus 14:24 says the LORD looked down on the Egyptian army from the pillar of fire and cloud and threw them into confusion. Psalm 18:14 says He shot His arrows and scattered the foes. Psalm 29:3 says the voice of the LORD is over the waters.
explore: Resounded
Gave out a loud voice; thunder is often called God's voice in the Psalms.
Arrows
Here a picture of lightning bolts darting through the sky.
verses.reflect: How does picturing God's power in a storm affect the way you face storms of life?
verses.alt: Lightning forking over a wild sea at night with rain sweeping across the water.

verses.title: The earth trembled
verses.heading: Thunder in the whirlwind
verses.meaning: Verse 18 says: 'Your thunder resounded in the whirlwind; the lightning lit up the world; the earth trembled and quaked.' The storm grows. Thunder rolls in the whirling wind, lightning lights up everything, and the ground itself shakes. Creation responds to God's presence like it did at Mount Sinai. The psalmist who could not sleep now sees God's majesty filling the world. The God who seemed absent fills heaven and earth.
verses.context: Exodus 19:16-18 describes thunder, lightning and the mountain trembling at Sinai. Psalm 97:4 says His lightning lights up the world and the earth sees and trembles. Hebrews 12:26 says His voice shook the earth.
explore: Whirlwind
A rolling or whirling storm; the word can also describe a turning wheel.
Quaked
Shook violently, as in an earthquake, the ground itself reacting to God's presence.
verses.reflect: When have you sensed God's presence as overwhelming rather than gentle?
verses.alt: A broad landscape lit white by lightning with hills and trees bending in the wind.

verses.title: Unseen footprints
verses.heading: A path through the sea
verses.meaning: Verse 19 says: 'Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters, but Your footprints were not to be found.' God made a road where there was no road. He led His people right through the sea. Yet His footprints could not be seen; the waters closed over the path. This is the psalm's great insight. God was present and leading even when no trace of Him was visible. The same was true in the psalmist's sleepless night.
verses.context: Isaiah 43:16 says the LORD makes a way through the sea. Exodus 14:29 says Israel walked on dry ground through the sea. Romans 11:33 says His ways are beyond tracing out.
explore: Mighty waters
Vast deep waters, a picture of overwhelming danger that God masters.
Footprints
Tracks or traces; God's path cannot be followed by sight, only by trust.
verses.reflect: Where might God be leading you now even though you can't see His footprints?
verses.alt: A dry path between walls of water with no tracks visible on the wet sand.

verses.title: Like a flock
verses.heading: Led by Moses and Aaron
verses.meaning: Verse 20 ends: 'You led Your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron.' After the storm comes a gentle picture. God guided His people like a shepherd leading sheep, using human leaders, Moses and Aaron, as His hands. The mighty God of thunder is also the tender Shepherd. The psalm ends without resolving every question, but with the assurance that God leads His people, often through ordinary people He sends.
verses.context: Psalm 78:52 says He led His people out like sheep through the wilderness. Isaiah 63:11-12 recalls God who brought them through the sea with the shepherd of His flock. John 10:11 says Jesus is the good shepherd.
explore: Flock
A herd of sheep or goats, a picture of God's people under His care.
By the hand of
Through the agency of; God worked through Moses and Aaron to lead Israel.
verses.reflect: Who has God used as a 'hand' to guide you, and how might you thank them?
verses.alt: A flock of sheep walking through a desert valley behind two shepherds with staffs.
